title: These Companies Raised Hundreds of Millions to Sell to LGBT People. Is the Money Really That Easy to Make?
excerpt: Everyone says it is a market worth trillions. The reality is far harder.
body:
Everyone says it is a market worth trillions. The reality is far harder.

Last Saturday, a hotel on Beijing's East Third Ring Road hosted a matchmaking event. It looked like any other blind-date gathering: long tables lined the banquet hall with chairs set facing each other, and more than 80 men and women queued for their numbers. On stage, the host explained the evening while asking attendees to fill in their details.

What set it apart was the questionnaire each person filled in after sitting down:

- How you plan to have children: A. Natural conception; B. Artificial insemination; C. IVF; D. Surrogacy; E. Adoption.
- Divorce: A. Divorce after a set number of years; B. Avoid divorce if possible.
- Preferred partner type: T; P; H; 1; 0; 0.5; G; no preference.

"I came with him today. His family is putting a lot of pressure on him. I'm not looking," said a young man who looked like a student. He had walked up to the *QDaily* reporter unprompted, and introduced the man of about 30 beside him.

The two are a couple. The older man is the youngest son in his family; both his elder brothers have married and had children, so his family has turned the pressure on him. But the couple want to stay together, and the only way out they could think of was to find a lesbian for a "form marriage."

A form marriage, as the name suggests, is a marriage in form only: a gay man and a lesbian register to marry, or carry a fake marriage certificate, to satisfy their families and their bosses.

This is not the same as the cases in the news where gay men deceive women into marrying them. A form marriage rests on both sides knowing the arrangement and agreeing to it. Even so, marriage in name only remains highly controversial, and the two parties may face real legal risks over property and over having and raising children.

But the people at this event wanted to get married first and worry about the risks later. As we talked with them, the social pressure they face came through again and again. Another young man we spoke with works at a state-owned enterprise. Because he has stayed single so long, he worries his boss will work out that he is gay and that it will hurt his chances of promotion. Pressure at work drove him to come looking for a form-marriage partner.

The event was organized by a Beijing start-up. It was the company's first form-marriage matchmaking event on this scale; before this, it had only run a few very small meet-ups.

That day the temperature in Beijing fell to minus 17 degrees Celsius, yet the room was packed. Latecomers found no seats and had to chat on the sofas along the wall.

The host on stage was the start-up's CEO himself. His pacing was off, but he worked hard to warm up the room. The company plans to raise the frequency of these events to two a month.

Homosexuality is discussed more and more openly, but, like homosexuality itself, form marriage is still not a topic everyone accepts. At the company's request, we have withheld its name.

## The "LGBT economy" is a pie in the sky drawn by investors

"Some people in society support form marriage and some oppose it. We do this because this group needs it," the CEO of the company behind the event told *QDaily*. The CEO is himself straight, married, with a child; he started the business mainly to make money by meeting a need.

Because the need is there, LGBT people were not the only ones in the room. Chunyu Doctor was there offering consultations on surrogacy and IVF, and so were lawyers who can sort out pre-marital property.

Businesses aimed at LGBT people have been under way for some time. China's gay-men's communities Blued and Zank are already experimenting with livestreaming, marketing and e-commerce. Two weeks ago, the Chinese gaming company Kunlun Tech paid US$93 million for 60% of Grindr, the world's largest gay dating app, and suddenly the LGBT economy was in the public eye.

Even research reports on the LGBT economy paint a very rosy picture of this group. The global LGBT consumer market is estimated to be worth about US$3.7 trillion, with the US market alone at US$885 billion.

When investors talk about the spending potential of LGBT people, the conclusion is always that they have more money and like to spend it. A report on Chinese gay consumers in *The Wall Street Journal* last year offered a typical case: Mr. Li (name transliterated), a 31-year-old human resources manager in Shanghai who uses a Sony phone, loves traveling abroad, and rarely thinks twice before buying something, all on an annual income of just 120,000 yuan.

LGBT Capital, a firm based in London and Hong Kong, puts China's gay market at as much as US$300 billion, second only to Europe and the United States.

According to [data from CMI](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/10491.html), a US firm that does LGBT market research and strategy consulting, every US$1 American businesses invest in the LGBT community returns US$180; for every US$158 that heterosexuals spend, gay people spend US$878, a gap of four to five times.

Generally speaking, LGBT people are more likely to be free of children and family pressure, put more weight on their careers, and earn more in China's first- and second-tier cities. So in their daily spending they care more about quality and prefer well-designed products.

But the picture investors paint of the LGBT economy still looks full of holes. One problem cannot be ignored: LGBT people are ordinary people first, and most of what they need for food, clothing, housing and getting around is probably no different from what any other consumer needs.

"Gongzi K" (a nickname), a music radio host in Fuzhou, told *QDaily* that he buys his everyday goods at Walmart or online, but because of his work he often orders books and CDs from overseas websites, and concerts are his biggest expense.

Gongzi K has not come out to his family, but he will not consider a form marriage and has decided to stay single for life. After rent, food and other living costs, he has 4,000 yuan a month to spend as he likes. He has long wanted to swap the iPhone 5 he bought two or three years ago for a 6s, but after going to Taylor Swift's Shanghai concert last year, he has had to watch his spending.

Among the people we interviewed, Gongzi K was no exception. Being LGBT does not mean shopping at special stores for special brands.

## These companies are doing business with LGBT people, but they have barely begun to tap this market

According to public figures, Grindr has 10 million registered users worldwide, and membership fees are its main source of revenue. China's two largest gay dating apps, Blued and Zank, claim 22 million and more than 10 million registered users respectively, covering almost every gay man in China who owns a smartphone. Population estimates put China's LGBT population at about 70 million, of whom around 30 million are gay men.

In China, the vast majority of LGBT people have not come out, so the internet is a good place for them to be active, swap information and find others like themselves. Its anonymity protects their privacy and makes it easier for them to find one another.

Having gathered these people in one place, social apps such as Blued and Zank have begun to look for ways to make money from them.

Liu Xin, head of marketing at Blued, told *QDaily* that the company began preparing to commercialize in the fourth quarter of last year and can now offer clients full-package campaigns: besides ad slots inside the app, these include offline events, WeChat and Weibo, and promotion through its own web series.

Blued has also begun testing livestreaming, the feature everyone is chasing right now. Its selling point is handsome men: no games, no pretty women, no talent required. Most streams show daily life, such as chatting, cooking and working out. To make the feature earn more, besides letting viewers send hosts virtual gifts such as chrysanthemums and cucumbers, Blued has started selling hosts "pin-to-top" cards: for 100 yuan a card, a host can push his channel to the top of the list.

![Blued launched livestreaming two weeks ago; users can buy Wandou credits to top up](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122947EbB0S2IumwfK1938.jpg-w600)

Zank, for its part, has turned to e-commerce. Last Dragon Boat Festival it launched "Zan Huo Selection," working with brands and service providers such as P&G and Meilijiafen. For now it mainly sends traffic to e-commerce platforms; the next version will bring more merchants onto the platform.

Investors have started moving into this field because they see that these online communities can pinpoint what gay people want, which also shows that the market has begun to go after gay people's spending power.

Chen Haozhi, head of commercial services at Zank, told *QDaily* that the gay-men's niche differs from niches such as mother-and-baby products. Mother-and-baby is a specialized need within the general population; Zank, by contrast, serves the general needs of gay men, which cover not only clothing, cosmetics and 3C products (computers, communications and consumer electronics) but also services such as beauty salons, haircuts and travel.

Tourism was one of the first industries to spot this opportunity, and among Zank's services, travel routes customized for gay people are the most popular. Zank CEO Ling Jueding told *QDaily* that at first the travel agencies came to Zank, wanting to design suitable routes for gay travelers. Besides providing a sign-up page, Zank also tells the agencies what to watch out for, such as which shops are a must and which are best avoided.

![Zank's service menu](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150947KYwp2C1VjPuOFIE6.jpg-w600)

Travel agencies that have their eye on the gay market include China International Travel Service and CYTS Tours. Zank has now agreed with them to pick packages from their offerings for its users to choose from.

Thailand, with its openness about sex and its range of services, has become the favorite destination of gay travelers in Asia. In Barcelona, the AXEL hotel group caters to LGBT guests, and in the United States, the cruise company Atlantis runs cruises exclusively for LGBT travelers.

Men's beauty and cosmetics may be the next opportunity. [Men care more and more about their looks](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/21012.html): in 2013, men's spending on cosmetics overtook shaving products for the first time, and the market research firm Mintel says that in 2013 sales of men's grooming products rose 3.4% to 30 million pounds, 5% of retail sales.

Anymood, a company that makes only men's cosmetics, built its first product around the pitch of a "BB cream that isn't girly." Wei Shi'erchu told *QDaily* that they chose to start with gay men because "in the past, (people thought) the first men to use facial cleanser were girly, but now it's completely normal. In the same way, the first men to use BB cream today are gay men."

![Anymood's [promotional copy](http://x.maka.im/pcviewer/E00KYI2P?DSCKID=0b17a89a-2e02-4a32-a479-8e19c48de23b&DSTIMESTAMP=1452928232484) is not aimed only at gay men](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150948zMvS1yiq7ga9XGNh.jpg-w600)

Gay men pay more attention to their appearance, and the fashion industry has always been dominated by gay people. To win this group's spending, what matters most is understanding what they actually need.

Some mainstream brands have begun making products with clear LGBT themes. In January last year, Tiffany, the 178-year-old jeweler, released its first engagement-ring ad featuring a same-sex couple.

![With this poster, Tiffany extended its customer base to same-sex couples](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150949rsYM82aWJ5ovmzfD.jpg-w600)

Marketing aimed at same-sex couples in China has also picked up. Last June, Taobao and Blued sent seven same-sex couples from China to Seattle to register their marriages. Taobao used the campaign to bring in sponsors and sold travel packages, home goods and more on the campaign page.

## But this business is actually hard

Ling Jueding, CEO of Zank, explains gay men's spending preferences this way: "None of these things have to be aimed at gay men; some designs just happen to suit gay men's taste. Apple (products), for example, aren't made for gay men, but our survey found that half of gay men use Apple, compared with only 30% of straight men. All we can conclude is that gay men like Apple's products more."

This is a problem common to companies doing LGBT business. It is not just brands and the general public: even the LGBT communities and service providers themselves have not worked out how to connect LGBT people with brands.

Part of the reason is that most LGBT people in China are still hidden. "Most gay people (in China) are still at the stage of accepting themselves. Most don't imagine their future lives; they only think about the present," Wei Shi'erchu, co-founder of Anymood, told *QDaily*, describing the situation of gay men today. "China's pink economy is built on the pink population accepting itself."

But for many LGBT people, the time to come out has not yet arrived, and as an invisible minority, they remain little understood by the outside world. Damien Lu, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who has long run a gay Q&A column on Aibai.com, believes that only when more people come out will real change follow.

Things may improve; at the least, we can already see some effort. After the US Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage last June, Ogilvy London set up Ogilvy Pride, a unit devoted to LGBT business. "With the trend toward legalizing same-sex marriage, the number of brands that want to do 'rainbow marketing' has soared," said Andrew Barratt, head of Ogilvy Pride.

More detailed services, better suited to LGBT people, are also being rolled out. LGBT Wealth, a business run by LGBT Capital, provides financial management and advice to sexual minorities. Because LGBT people lack the protection of marriage, they have particular needs when it comes to property shared with partners, financial planning and retirement.

Of course, all this is just the beginning. For most of the start-ups that have rushed into this market with venture capital in hand, a slow start may prove fatal.

Cover image: a still from [*Queer as Folk*](http://outtv.ca/shows/queer-as-folk-uk/)
